Approach: # Minimum Dominating Set The following Rust code solves the Minimum Dominating Set problem using a greedy algorithm. The algorithm works by iteratively selecting the vertex that covers the most uncovered vertices. ## Code

View Rust Code (3588 chars)
use std::collections::{HashSet, VecDeque};
use std::io::{self, BufRead};

/// Represents an undirected graph using an adjacency list.
struct Graph {
    num_vertices: usize,
    adjacency_list: Vec<Vec<usize>>,
}

impl Graph {
    /// Creates a new graph with the given number of vertices.
    fn new(num_vertices: usize) -> Self {
        Graph {
            num_vertices,
            adjacency_list: vec![vec![]; num_vertices],
        }
    }

    /// Adds an edge to the graph.
    fn add_edge(&mut self, u: usize, v: usize) {
        self.adjacency_list[u].push(v);
        self.adjacency_list[v].push(u);
    }

    /// Finds a minimum dominating set using a greedy algorithm.
    fn min_dominating_set(&self) -> HashSet<usize> {
        let mut dominating_set = HashSet::new();
        let mut covered = HashSet::new();
        let mut queue = VecDeque::new();

        // Initialize the queue with all vertices.
        for i in 0..self.num_vertices {
            queue.push_back(i);
        }

        while !queue.is_empty() {
            // Find the vertex that covers the most uncovered vertices.
            let mut max_vertex = None;
            let mut max_covered = 0;

            for _ in 0..queue.len() {
                let vertex = queue.pop_front().unwrap();
                let mut covered_count = 0;

                // Count the number of uncovered neighbors.
                for neighbor in &self.adjacency_list[vertex] {
                    if !covered.contains(neighbor) {
                        covered_count += 1;
                    }
                }

                if !covered.contains(&vertex) {
                    covered_count += 1;
                }

                if covered_count > max_covered {
                    max_vertex = Some(vertex);
                    max_covered = covered_count;
                }

                queue.push_back(vertex);
            }

            if let Some(max_vertex) = max_vertex {
                // Add the vertex to the dominating set and mark its neighbors as covered.
                dominating_set.insert(max_vertex);
                covered.insert(max_vertex);

                for neighbor in &self.adjacency_list[max_vertex] {
                    covered.insert(*neighbor);
                }

                // Remove the vertex from the queue.
                queue.retain(|&x| x != max_vertex);
            }
        }

        dominating_set
    }
}

fn main() {
    let stdin = io::stdin();
    let mut lines = stdin.lock().lines();

    // Read the number of vertices and edges.
    let first_line = lines.next().unwrap().unwrap();
    let mut parts = first_line.split_whitespace();
    let num_vertices: usize = parts.next().unwrap().parse().unwrap();
    let num_edges: usize = parts.next().unwrap().parse().unwrap();

    // Create a new graph.
    let mut graph = Graph::new(num_vertices);

    // Read the edges and add them to the graph.
    for _ in 0..num_edges {
        let line = lines.next().unwrap().unwrap();
        let mut parts = line.split_whitespace();
        let u: usize = parts.next().unwrap().parse().unwrap();
        let v: usize = parts.next().unwrap().parse().unwrap();

        graph.add_edge(u, v);
    }

    // Find the minimum dominating set.
    let dominating_set = graph.min_dominating_set();

    // Print the size and vertices of the dominating set.
    println!("{}", dominating_set.len());
    print!("{}", dominating_set.iter().next().unwrap());
    for vertex in dominating_set.iter().skip(1) {
        print!(" {}", vertex);
    }
    println!();
}

Here, we provide a C++ solution using a brute-force approach with bit manipulation to generate all possible subsets of vertices and check if they form an independen...

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <cstdint>
#include <algorithm>
#include <stdexcept>

// Structure to represent an undirected graph using adjacency list
class Graph {
public:
    Graph(int n) : numVertices(n), adjList(n) {}

    void addEdge(int u, int v) {
        adjList[u].push_back(v);
        adjList[v].push_back(u);
    }

    bool isIndependentSet(uint64_t subset) const {
        for (int i = 0; i < numVertices; ++i) {
            if ((subset & (1ULL << i)) != 0) {
                for (const auto& neighbor : adjList[i]) {
                    if ((subset & (1ULL << neighbor)) != 0) {
                        return false;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return true;
    }

    int countSetBits(uint64_t n) const {
        int count = 0;
        while (n) {
            count += n & 1;
            n >>= 1;
        }
        return count;
    }

    std::vector<int> getMaxIndependentSet() const {
        uint64_t maxSubset = 0;
        int maxSize = 0;

        // Iterate over all possible subsets
        for (uint64_t subset = 0; subset < (1ULL << numVertices); ++subset) {
            if (isIndependentSet(subset)) {
                int size = countSetBits(subset);
                if (size > maxSize) {
                    maxSize = size;
                    maxSubset = subset;
                }
            }
        }

        // Extract vertices from the maximum independent set
        std::vector<int> maxIndependentSet;
        for (int i = 0; i < numVertices; ++i) {
            if ((maxSubset & (1ULL << i)) != 0) {
                maxIndependentSet.push_back(i);
            }
        }

        return maxIndependentSet;
    }

private:
    int numVertices;
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adjList;
};

int main() {
    try {
        int n, m;
        std::cin >> n >> m;

        if (n < 0 || m < 0) {
            throw std::invalid_argument("Number of vertices and edges must be non-negative.");
        }

        Graph graph(n);

        for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
            int u, v;
            std::cin >> u >> v;

            if (u < 0 || v < 0 || u >= n || v >= n) {
                throw std::out_of_range("Vertex index out of range.");
            }

            graph.addEdge(u, v);
        }

        std::vector<int> maxIndependentSet = graph.getMaxIndependentSet();

        // Output the size and vertices of the maximum independent set
        std::cout << maxIndependentSet.size() << std::endl;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < maxIndependentSet.size(); ++i) {
            std::cout << maxIndependentSet[i];
            if (i != maxIndependentSet.size() - 1) {
                std::cout << " ";
            }
        }
        std::cout << std::endl;

        return 0;
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cerr << "Error: " << e.what() << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }
}

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <cstdint>
#include <algorithm>

// Structure to represent an undirected graph using adjacency list
class Graph {
public:
    Graph(int n) : numVertices(n), adjList(n) {}

    void addEdge(int u, int v) {
        adjList[u].push_back(v);
        adjList[v].push_back(u);
    }

    bool isIndependentSet(uint64_t subset) const {
        for (int i = 0; i < numVertices; ++i) {
            if ((subset & (1ULL << i)) != 0) {
                for (const auto& neighbor : adjList[i]) {
                    if ((subset & (1ULL << neighbor)) != 0) {
                        return false;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return true;
    }

    int countSetBits(uint64_t n) const {
        int count = 0;
        while (n) {
            count += n & 1;
            n >>= 1;
        }
        return count;
    }

    std::vector<int> getMaxIndependentSet() const {
        uint64_t maxSubset = 0;
        int maxSize = 0;

        // Iterate over all possible subsets
        for (uint64_t subset = 0; subset < (1ULL << numVertices); ++subset) {
            if (isIndependentSet(subset)) {
                int size = countSetBits(subset);
                if (size > maxSize) {
                    maxSize = size;
                    maxSubset = subset;
                }
            }
        }

        // Extract vertices from the maximum independent set
        std::vector<int> maxIndependentSet;
        for (int i = 0; i < numVertices; ++i) {
            if ((maxSubset & (1ULL << i)) != 0) {
                maxIndependentSet.push_back(i);
            }
        }

        return maxIndependentSet;
    }

private:
    int numVertices;
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adjList;
};

        std::cin >> n >> m;

You are writing C# code to solve the **Directed Feedback Vertex Set** problem.

Given a directed graph, find the smallest set of vertices to remove so the remaining graph has **no directed cycles** (i.e., it becomes a DAG).

**Input format (stdin)**

n m
u v
u v
... (m lines total)
```
- `n`: number of vertices (0-indexed: `0..n-1`)
- `m`: number of directed edges
- each line `u v` means an edge `u -> v`

**Output format (stdout)**

k

```
- `k`: number of removed vertices
- second line: exactly `k` distinct vertex indices (any order)

**What is checked**
1. Output format is valid.
2. Vertex indices are valid and distinct.
3. Removing those vertices makes the graph acyclic.
4. The set size is minimum.

Approach: # Directed Feedback Vertex Set Problem Solution The Directed Feedback Vertex Set problem is a well-known NP-hard problem. We will use a brute-force approach with some optimizations to solve it. ## Code

View C# Code (3656 chars)
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.IO;
using System.Linq;

public class DirectedFeedbackVertexSet
{
    private static bool IsAcyclic(bool[][] graph, bool[] removed)
    {
        int n = graph.Length;
        int[] inDegree = new int[n];

        // Calculate in-degree of each vertex
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        {
            if (!removed[i])
            {
                foreach (int neighbor in Enumerable.Range(0, n).Where(j => graph[i][j]))
                {
                    if (!removed[neighbor])
                    {
                        inDegree[neighbor]++;
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        // Initialize queue with vertices having in-degree 0
        Queue<int> queue = new Queue<int>(Enumerable.Range(0, n).Where(i => !removed[i] && inDegree[i] == 0));

        int visitedCount = 0;
        while (queue.Count > 0)
        {
            int vertex = queue.Dequeue();
            visitedCount++;

            foreach (int neighbor in Enumerable.Range(0, n).Where(j => graph[vertex][j]))
            {
                if (!removed[neighbor])
                {
                    inDegree[neighbor]--;
                    if (inDegree[neighbor] == 0)
                    {
                        queue.Enqueue(neighbor);
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        // If all non-removed vertices are visited, then the graph is acyclic
        return visitedCount == Enumerable.Range(0, n).Count(i => !removed[i]);
    }

    private static List<int> FindMinFeedbackVertexSet(bool[][] graph)
    {
        int n = graph.Length;
        int minSize = n;
        List<int> minSet = new List<int>(n);

        // Iterate over all possible subsets of vertices
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++)
        {
            bool[] removed = new bool[n];
            int count = 0;

            // Create a subset of vertices to remove based on the current mask
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            {
                if ((mask & (1 << i)) != 0)
                {
                    removed[i] = true;
                    count++;
                }
            }

            // Check if removing the current subset makes the graph acyclic
            if (IsAcyclic(graph, removed))
            {
                // Update the minimum-size set if the current subset is smaller
                if (count < minSize)
                {
                    minSize = count;
                    minSet = Enumerable.Range(0, n).Where(i => removed[i]).ToList();
                }
            }
        }

        return minSet;
    }

    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        using (StreamReader reader = new StreamReader(Console.OpenStandardInput()))
        using (StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter(Console.OpenStandardOutput()))
        {
            string[] line = reader.ReadLine().Split();
            int n = int.Parse(line[0]);
            int m = int.Parse(line[1]);

            bool[][] graph = new bool[n][];

            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            {
                graph[i] = new bool[n];
            }

            for (int i = 0; i < m; i++)
            {
                line = reader.ReadLine().Split();
                int u = int.Parse(line[0]);
                int v = int.Parse(line[1]);

                graph[u][v] = true;
            }

            List<int> feedbackVertexSet = FindMinFeedbackVertexSet(graph);

            writer.WriteLine(feedbackVertexSet.Count);
            writer.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", feedbackVertexSet));
        }
    }
}

            int m = int.Parse(line[1]);

            bool[][] graph = new bool[n][];

            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            {
                graph[i] = new bool[n];
            }

            for (int i = 0; i < m; i++)
            {
                line = reader.ReadLine().Split();
                int u = int.Parse(line[0]);
                int v = int.Parse(line[1]);

                graph[u][v] = true;
            }

            List<int> feedbackVertexSet = FindMinFeedbackVertexSet(graph);

            writer.WriteLine(feedbackVertexSet.Count);
            writer.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", feedbackVertexSet));
        }

Given a universe of elements and a list of sets, we need to choose set indices such that every element is covered exactly once. Key constraints and edge cases: - The input format is given as `U S` followed by `S` lines, where each line represents a set containing space-separated element IDs. - `U` is the number of elements...

View Python Code (1233 chars)
def exact_cover(U, sets):
    def backtrack(index, covered, chosen):
        if len(covered) == U:
            return chosen
        if index == len(sets):
            return None
        # Try including the current set
        new_covered = covered.copy()
        valid = True
        for elem in sets[index]:
            if elem in new_covered:
                valid = False
                break
            new_covered.add(elem)
        if valid:
            result = backtrack(index + 1, new_covered, chosen + [index])
            if result is not None:
                return result
        # Try excluding the current set
        return backtrack(index + 1, covered, chosen)
    result = backtrack(0, set(), [])
    if result is None:
        return "NO SOLUTION"
    else:
        return "SOLUTION\n" + ' '.join(map(str, result))

def main():
    try:
        U, S = map(int, input().split())
        sets = []
        for _ in range(S):
            sets.append(list(map(int, input().split())))
        print(exact_cover(U, sets))
    except EOFError:
        print("NO SOLUTION", file=sys.stderr)
    except ValueError:
        print("Invalid input format", file=sys.stderr)

import sys
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::io::{self, BufRead};

fn main() {
    let stdin = io::stdin();
    let mut lines = stdin.lock().lines().map(|l| l.unwrap());

    let first_line: Vec<i32> = lines.next().unwrap().split_whitespace()
        .map(|x| x.parse().unwrap()).collect();
    let n = first_line[0] as usize;
    let m = first_line[1] as usize;

    let mut graph = vec![vec![]; n];
    for line in lines.take(m) {
        let edge: Vec<usize> = line.split_whitespace()
            .map(|x| x.parse().unwrap()).collect();
        let u = edge[0];
        let v = edge[1];
        graph[u].push(v);
        graph[v].push(u);
    }

    let mut min_cut = std::usize::MAX;
    let mut best_partition: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();

    for mask in 0..(1 << n) {
        let mut partition_a = Vec::new();
        for i in 0..n {
            if (mask & (1 << i)) != 0 {
                partition_a.push(i);
            }
        }
        if partition_a.len() == n / 2 {
            let cut_size = calculate_cut_size(&graph, &partition_a);
            if cut_size < min_cut {
                min_cut = cut_size;
                best_partition = partition_a.clone();
            }
        }
    }

    println!("{}", min_cut);
    println!("{}", best_partition.iter().map(|x| x.to_string()).collect::<Vec<String>>().join(" "));
}

fn calculate_cut_size(graph: &Vec<Vec<usize>>, partition_a: &Vec<usize>) -> usize {
    let mut cut_size = 0;
    let partition_a_set: HashSet<usize> = partition_a.iter().cloned().collect();
    for &u in partition_a {
        for &v in &graph[u] {
            if !partition_a_set.contains(&v) {
                cut_size += 1;
            }
        }
    }
    cut_size / 2 // Because each edge is counted twice
}

def solve_ilp(n, m, c, constraints):
    max_objective = float('-inf')
    best_assignment = None
    for assignment in generate_assignments(n):
        if is_feasible(assignment, constraints):
            objective = calculate_objective(c, assignment)
            if objective > max_objective:
                max_objective = objective
                best_assignment = assignment
    return max_objective, best_assignment

def generate_assignments(n):
    for i in range(2**n):
        assignment = [int(b) for b in bin(i)[2:].zfill(n)]
        yield assignment

def is_feasible(assignment, constraints):
    for u, v in constraints:
        if assignment[u] + assignment[v] > 1:
            return False
    return True

def calculate_objective(c, assignment):
    return sum(ci * xi for ci, xi in zip(c, assignment))

Typical Prompt:
You are writing a SPIR-V assembly text fragment shader. The shader will be assembled
with spirv-as (Vulkan 1.0 target) and rendered on a unit sphere.

**Available inputs (from vertex shader):**
```
layout(location = 0) in vec3 worldPos; ; world-space position
layout(location = 1) in vec3 normal; ; world-space normal (interpolated, may need normalize)
layout(location = 2) in vec2 uv; ; texture coordinates in [0,1]
layout(location = 3) in vec3 tangent; ; tangent vector
layout(location = 4) in vec3 color; ; per-vertex color (smoothly varies: typical value: rgb = 0.5+0.5*xyz)
```

**Available uniform buffer (DescriptorSet 0, Binding 0):**
```
struct UBO { // std140 layout
mat4 model; // offset 0 (column-major)
mat4 view; // offset 64
mat4 projection; // offset 128
vec4 lightPos; // offset 192 -- typical value: (5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 1.0)
vec4 cameraPos; // offset 208 -- typical value: (0.0, 0.0, 3.0, 1.0)
vec4 params; // offset 224 -- typical value: (0.0, 0.5, 0.0, 0.0)
};
```

**Required output:**
```
layout(location = 0) out vec4 outColor; RGBA float, will be stored as rgba8unorm
```

**SPIR-V requirements:**
- Start with `; SPIR-V` header comment and version
- Use `OpCapability Shader` and `OpMemoryModel Logical GLSL450`
- Use `OpEntryPoint Fragment %main "main"` listing ALL input/output variables used
- Use `OpExecutionMode %main OriginUpperLeft`
- Declare all necessary decorations (Location, DescriptorSet, Binding, Block, Offsets)
- All input variables are `Input` storage class, output is `Output` storage class
- The uniform buffer variable is `Uniform` storage class
- Entry point function name must be "main"

**Write ONLY the complete SPIR-V assembly text.** Do not include any other text or explanation
outside the SPIR-V text.


**Task:** Output a solid red color (vec4(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)).
 Prompt Changes:
Prompt parameters change between subpasses (increasing difficulty)

Test 42: Geometry Shaders (SPIR-V Assembly) Score: 1.00 / 15
Typical Prompt:
You are writing a SPIR-V assembly geometry shader. It will be assembled with
spirv-as (Vulkan 1.0) and rendered using a fixed vertex shader and fragment shader.

**Geometry shader requirements:**
- `OpCapability Geometry`
- `OpMemoryModel Logical GLSL450`
- `OpEntryPoint Geometry %main "main"` listing ALL interface variables
- `OpExecutionMode %main ` (InputPoints/InputLines/Triangles/InputLinesAdjacency/InputTrianglesAdjacency)
- `OpExecutionMode %main ` (OutputPoints/OutputLineStrip/OutputTriangleStrip)
- `OpExecutionMode %main OutputVertices ` (max vertices emitted)
- `OpExecutionMode %main Invocations 1`

**Input from vertex shader (per-vertex arrays):**
The input gl_Position is in a gl_PerVertex block (must be decorated with Block + BuiltIn Position).
```
%gl_PerVertex_in = OpTypeStruct %v4float
OpDecorate %gl_PerVertex_in Block
OpMemberDecorate %gl_PerVertex_in 0 BuiltIn Position
; Array size depends on input primitive:
; InputPoints: 1, InputLines: 2, Triangles: 3
; InputLinesAdjacency: 4, InputTrianglesAdjacency: 6
%arr_pv_in = OpTypeArray %gl_PerVertex_in %uint_N
%ptr_in_arr_pv = OpTypePointer Input %arr_pv_in
%gl_in = OpVariable %ptr_in_arr_pv Input
; Access: OpAccessChain %ptr_in_v4 %gl_in %int_i %int_0 -> gl_in[i].gl_Position
```

User-defined inputs are also arrays of the same size:
```
layout(location = 0) in vec3 worldPos[]; ; positions in clip space
layout(location = 1) in vec3 normal[]; ; vertex normals
layout(location = 2) in vec3 color[]; ; per-vertex colors
```

**Output (per emitted vertex):**
The output gl_Position is in a gl_PerVertex block:
```
%gl_PerVertex_out = OpTypeStruct %v4float
OpDecorate %gl_PerVertex_out Block
OpMemberDecorate %gl_PerVertex_out 0 BuiltIn Position
%ptr_out_pv = OpTypePointer Output %gl_PerVertex_out
%gl_out = OpVariable %ptr_out_pv Output
; Store: OpAccessChain %ptr_out_v4 %gl_out %int_0 -> gl_out.gl_Position
```
```
layout(location = 0) out vec3 outColor; ; color for fragment shader
```

**Emit vertices with:** `OpEmitVertex` after storing gl_Position and outColor.
**End primitive with:** `OpEndPrimitive` after emitting a complete strip.

**Available UBO (set=0, binding=0) - accessible from geometry shader:**
Same layout as test 41 (model/view/proj matrices, lightPos, cameraPos, params).

**Write ONLY the complete SPIR-V assembly text for the geometry shader.**


**Input primitive:** InputPoints (1 vertex per invocation, array size 1)
**Geometry:** 25 colored points in a 5x5 grid spread across [-0.8, 0.8].

**Task:** Expand each point into a small colored quad (4 vertices as triangle strip).
1. Read gl_in[0].gl_Position (the point position).
2. Read color[0] (the point's color).
3. Define a half-size: h = 0.04.
4. Emit 4 vertices forming a quad centered on the point:
- (x-h, y-h), (x+h, y-h), (x-h, y+h), (x+h, y+h)
- All with z=0, w=1, and the same color.
5. Output as triangle strip, max 4 vertices.
 Prompt Changes:
Prompt parameters change between subpasses (increasing difficulty)

struct PSInput {

[[vk::location(1)]] float3 normal : TEXCOORD1; // world-space normal (interpolated, may need normalize)
[[vk::location(2)]] float2 uv : TEXCOORD2; // texture coordinates in [0,1]
[[vk::location(3)]] float3 tangent : TEXCOORD3; // tangent vector
[[vk::location(4)]] float3 color : TEXCOORD4; // per-vertex color (smoothly varies: rgb = 0.5+0.5*xyz)
};

float4x4 view; // offset 64

float4 cameraPos; // value: (0.0, 0.0, 3.0, 1.0)
float4 params; // value: (0.0, 0.5, 0.0, 0.0)
};

**Required output:**

float4 main(PSInput input) : SV_Target0 // RGBA float, stored as rgba8unorm

cbuffer UBO : register(b0) {
    float4x4 model;          // offset 0   (column-major)
    float4x4 view;           // offset 64
    float4x4 projection;     // offset 128
    float4 lightPos;         // value: (5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 1.0)
    float4 cameraPos;        // value: (0.0, 0.0, 3.0, 1.0)
    float4 params;           // value: (0.0, 0.5, 0.0, 0.0)
};

struct PSInput {
    [[vk::location(0)]] float3 worldPos : TEXCOORD0;   // world-space position
    [[vk::location(1)]] float3 normal   : TEXCOORD1;   // world-space normal (interpolated, may need normalize)
    [[vk::location(2)]] float2 uv       : TEXCOORD2;   // texture coordinates in [0,1]
    [[vk::location(3)]] float3 tangent  : TEXCOORD3;   // tangent vector
    [[vk::location(4)]] float3 color    : TEXCOORD4;   // per-vertex color (smoothly varies: rgb = 0.5+0.5*xyz)
};

float4 main(PSInput input) : SV_Target0 {
    float2 c = float2(input.uv.x * 3.0 - 2.0, input.uv.y * 2.0 - 1.0);
    float2 z = float2(0.0, 0.0);
    uint iterations = 0;
    for (uint i = 0; i < 20; ++i) {
        z = float2(z.x * z.x - z.y * z.y, 2.0 * z.x * z.y) + c;
        if (dot(z, z) > 4.0) break;
        ++iterations;
    }
    float t = float(iterations) / 20.0;
    return float4(t, t * 0.5, 1.0 - t, 1.0);
}

    [[vk::location(3)]] float3 tangent  : TEXCOORD3;   
    [[vk::location(4)]] float3 color    : TEXCOORD4;   
};

float4 main(PSInput input) : SV_Target0 {
    float3 N = normalize(input.normal);
    float3 L = normalize(lightPos.xyz - input.worldPos);
    float3 V = normalize(cameraPos.xyz - input.worldPos);
    float3 R = reflect(-L, N);

    float3 ambient = float3(0.1, 0.05, 0.05);
    float3 diffuse = input.color * max(dot(N, L), 0);
    float3 specular = float3(1, 1, 1) * pow(max(dot(R, V), 0), 32);

    float3 color = ambient + diffuse + specular;
    color = clamp(color, 0, 1);

    return float4(color, 1.0);
}

    float t = float(iterations) / 20.0;
    outColor = vec4(t, t * 0.5, 1.0 - t, 1.0);
}

You are writing a SPIR-V fragment shader as raw binary data, encoded as a hex string.
The binary will be decoded from hex, validated with spirv-val, and rendered on a unit sphere.

**SPIR-V Binary Format (little-endian 32-bit words):**
Each 32-bit word is 8 hex characters (little-endian byte order).

Header (5 words):
```
03022307 // Magic number 0x07230203 (little-endian)
00000100 // Version 1.0 (0x00010000)
00000000 // Generator (0 = manual)
BBBBBBBB // Bound (max ID + 1)
00000000 // Reserved
```

Instructions follow as: first word = (WordCount << 16) | Opcode, then operands.

**Key opcodes (decimal):**
- OpCapability (17): word_count=2, operand=capability (1=Shader)
- OpExtInstImport (11): result_id, name_string
- OpMemoryModel (14): word_count=3, addressing=0(Logical), model=1(GLSL450)
- OpEntryPoint (15): execution_model=4(Fragment), entry_id, name, interface_vars...
- OpExecutionMode (16): entry_id, mode=7(OriginUpperLeft)
- OpDecorate (71): target, decoration, operands
- OpTypeVoid (19), OpTypeFunction (33), OpTypeFloat (22), OpTypeVector (23)
- OpTypePointer (32), OpVariable (59), OpConstant (43)
- OpFunction (54), OpFunctionEnd (56), OpLabel (248)
- OpLoad (61), OpStore (62), OpReturn (253)
- OpCompositeConstruct (80), OpCompositeExtract (81)
- OpDot (148), OpFMul (133), OpFAdd (129), OpFSub (131), OpFNegate (127)
- OpExtInst (12): GLSL.std.450 ext instructions

**Decoration values:** Location=30, DescriptorSet=34, Binding=33, Block=2, Offset=35

**Available inputs (from vertex shader):**
```
location 0: vec3 worldPos
location 1: vec3 normal
location 2: vec2 uv
location 3: vec3 tangent
location 4: vec3 color
```

**UBO (set=0, binding=0):** mat4 model(0), mat4 view(64), mat4 projection(128),
vec4 lightPos(192), vec4 cameraPos(208), vec4 params(224).

**Required output:** location 0: vec4 outColor

**Write ONLY the complete hex string of the SPIR-V binary.** Each byte as two hex
characters, no spaces or newlines within the hex data. The hex string represents
the raw bytes of the .spv file.

Test 46: N-Body Gravitational Simulation (GLSL Compute) Score: 0.00 / 6
Typical Prompt:
Write a GLSL compute shader for gravitational N-body simulation.

**GLSL Compute Shader Interface:**

```
#version 450

layout(local_size_x = 256) in;

// Each body is stored as two consecutive vec4s:
// vec4(position.xyz, mass)
// vec4(velocity.xyz, 0.0)
// So body i starts at index i*2 in the buffer.

layout(set = 0, binding = 0) readonly buffer InputBodies {
vec4 inData[]; // length = N * 2
};

layout(set = 0, binding = 1) buffer OutputBodies {
vec4 outData[]; // length = N * 2
};

layout(set = 0, binding = 2) uniform Params {
uvec4 counts; // counts.x = N (number of bodies)
vec4 physics; // physics.x = dt, physics.y = softening, physics.z = G
};
```

**Task:** Write a compute shader that performs ONE timestep of gravitational
N-body simulation using the leapfrog/Euler integration method. Each invocation
handles one body (gl_GlobalInvocationID.x), reading its position and velocity
from inData and writing updated values to outData. The acceleration should be
computed from all other bodies using:

acc += G * mass_j * (pos_j - pos_i) / (|pos_j - pos_i|^2 + softening^2)^(3/2)

Velocity is advanced by acc * dt and position is advanced by vel * dt. The
shader will be dispatched ceil(N/256) workgroups in X and run multiple times
with ping-pong buffers for the required number of timesteps.

**Critical Requirements:**
- Guard against gl_GlobalInvocationID.x >= N
- Use the softening parameter to avoid singularities
- Skip self-interaction (i == j)
- Write BOTH position+mass and velocity vec4s to output


**Test Configurations:**
Subpass 0: N=64, timesteps=10, dt=0.001, softening=0.01
Subpass 1: N=128, timesteps=20, dt=0.001, softening=0.01
Subpass 2: N=256, timesteps=50, dt=0.001, softening=0.01
Subpass 3: N=512, timesteps=100, dt=0.001, softening=0.01
Subpass 4: N=1024, timesteps=100, dt=0.001, softening=0.01
Subpass 5: N=2048, timesteps=200, dt=0.001, softening=0.01

G = 0.006674 (scaled gravitational constant)

Write the complete GLSL compute shader source code.

Test 47: Hash Mining / Proof of Work (WGSL Compute) Score: 0.00 / 5
Typical Prompt:
Write a WGSL compute shader for hash mining (proof-of-work).

**WGSL Compute Shader Interface:**

```wgsl
@group(0) @binding(0) var baseData : array;
@group(0) @binding(1) var result : array;
@group(0) @binding(2) var params : vec4;
// params.x = difficulty, params.y = range_start, params.z = range_size

@compute @workgroup_size(256)
fn main(@builtin(global_invocation_id) gid : vec3) { ... }
```

**Task:** Write a compute shader that searches for a uint32 nonce such that
the custom hash of (baseData XOR nonce) has at least `difficulty` trailing
zero bits in the 64-bit output.

**Hash function (MUST match exactly):**
```
function custom_hash(data[16], nonce) -> (h0, h1):
state[0..15] = data[0..15]
for i in 0..15: state[i] ^= (nonce + i)

// 8 rounds of quarter-round mixing (ChaCha-like)
repeat 8 times:
for each group of 4 consecutive elements (i, i+1, i+2, i+3):
a += b; d ^= a; d = rotl(d, 16)
c += d; b ^= c; b = rotl(b, 12)
a += b; d ^= a; d = rotl(d, 8)
c += d; b ^= c; b = rotl(b, 7)

// Fold 16 words to 2:
h0 = state[0] ^ state[2] ^ state[4] ^ state[6] ^ state[8] ^ state[10] ^ state[12] ^ state[14]
h1 = state[1] ^ state[3] ^ state[5] ^ state[7] ^ state[9] ^ state[11] ^ state[13] ^ state[15]
return (h0, h1) // h0 is low 32 bits
```

**Trailing zero count:** Count trailing zero bits of the 64-bit value [h0 | (h1 << 32)].
That is, count from h0's LSB first; if h0 == 0, add 32 and continue counting from h1.

**Algorithm:**
1. Each thread computes: my_nonce = params.y + gid.x (range_start + thread ID)
2. Guard: if gid.x >= params.z, return (out of range)
3. Compute hash, count trailing zeros
4. If trailing_zeros >= difficulty:
Write result[0]=1u, result[1]=nonce, result[2]=h0, result[3]=h1
(Race writes are acceptable - any valid nonce will be verified on CPU)

**Important WGSL notes:**
- Use `var state : array` for the mutable hash state.
- WGSL rotation: `(x << shift) | (x >> (32u - shift))` — all values must be u32.
- The inner quarter-round loop MUST be unrolled (write out all 4 groups
of state[0..3], state[4..7], state[8..11], state[12..15] explicitly).
- Do NOT use atomics. Plain stores to result[] are sufficient.
- All integer literals must be typed: use `0u`, `1u`, `16u`, `32u` etc.

The shader will be dispatched with ceil(range_size / 256) workgroups.
Only ONE dispatch is performed - find the nonce in a single pass.

Test 48: 2D Fluid Simulation - Lattice Boltzmann (SPIR-V ASM Compute) Score: 0.00 / 5
Typical Prompt:
Write a SPIR-V assembly compute shader for 2D Lattice Boltzmann fluid simulation.

**SPIR-V Assembly Compute Shader Interface:**

The shader uses the D2Q9 Lattice Boltzmann model for 2D fluid simulation.

**D2Q9 velocity directions (index k -> (cx, cy)):**
```
k=0: ( 0, 0) w=4/9 (rest)
k=1: ( 1, 0) w=1/9 (east)
k=2: ( 0, 1) w=1/9 (north)
k=3: (-1, 0) w=1/9 (west)
k=4: ( 0,-1) w=1/9 (south)
k=5: ( 1, 1) w=1/36 (NE)
k=6: (-1, 1) w=1/36 (NW)
k=7: (-1,-1) w=1/36 (SW)
k=8: ( 1,-1) w=1/36 (SE)
```

**Buffer layout:**
- Binding 0 (storage, read-only): float array, length W*H*9
Index = (y * W + x) * 9 + k
- Binding 1 (storage, read-write): float array, length W*H*9 (output, NOT writeonly)
- Binding 2 (uniform): { uvec4(W, H, 0, 0), vec4(omega, 0, 0, 0) }

**Algorithm (per cell at gl_GlobalInvocationID.xy):**
Compute one LBM step (collision + streaming) for each lattice cell. Guard against
out-of-bounds (x >= W or y >= H). For the cell distributions f[0..8], compute
macroscopic density rho and velocity (ux, uy) using the D2Q9 directions. Apply
the BGK collision update with:

cu = cx[k]*ux + cy[k]*uy
feq = w[k] * rho * (1 + 3*cu + 4.5*cu*cu - 1.5*(ux*ux + uy*uy))
f_out = f[k] + omega * (feq - f[k])

Then stream each f_out to the neighbor cell (x+cx[k], y+cy[k]) with periodic
wraparound in both axes. Write to the output buffer at the corresponding
neighbor index for k.

**SPIR-V requirements:**
- OpCapability Shader
- OpExecutionMode with LocalSize 16 16 1
- Use gl_GlobalInvocationID for (x, y)
- Declare runtime arrays for storage buffers with OpDecorate ArrayStride 4
- Use OpSMod or manual modulo for periodic boundary conditions

Test 49: Parallel Prefix Sum (SPIR-V Binary Compute) Score: 0.00 / 5
Typical Prompt:
Write a SPIR-V binary compute shader (hex-encoded) for parallel inclusive prefix sum.

**SPIR-V Binary (hex-encoded) Compute Shader Interface:**

You must produce raw SPIR-V binary encoded as a hex string (no spaces, no 0x prefix).
The binary must start with the SPIR-V magic number 0x07230203.

**Required layout:**
```
Binding 0 (set=0): Storage buffer (read-only) - uint array, length N
Binding 1 (set=0): Storage buffer (read-write) - uint array, length N
Binding 2 (set=0): Uniform buffer - uint4: [N, 0, 0, 0]

Local size: 256 x 1 x 1
```

**Algorithm:** Inclusive prefix sum (scan)
- Input: [a0, a1, a2, a3, ...]
- Output: [a0, a0+a1, a0+a1+a2, a0+a1+a2+a3, ...]

Compute an inclusive scan over the input array. For N <= 256, use a shared-memory
scan within a single workgroup (synchronize as needed). For N > 256, a naive
fallback (each thread sums all previous elements) is acceptable but slow; full
marks require a multi-workgroup scan.

**SPIR-V binary encoding notes:**
- Little-endian uint32 words
- Magic: 0x07230203
- Version: 0x00010000 (1.0)
- Bound: upper bound on all IDs used + 1
- Schema: 0
- OpCapability Shader = [0x00020011, 0x00000001]
- OpMemoryModel Logical GLSL450 = [0x00030006, 0x00000001, 0x00000001]
- OpEntryPoint GLCompute = opcode 0x0000000F, execution model 5
- OpExecutionMode LocalSize = opcode 0x00000010, mode 17 (LocalSize)
- OpDecorate Binding = decoration 33
- OpDecorate DescriptorSet = decoration 34
- OpDecorate ArrayStride = decoration 6
- OpDecorate BufferBlock or Block = decoration 2 or 3
- OpTypeInt 32 0 = unsigned int
- OpTypePointer StorageBuffer = storage class 12
- OpVariable StorageBuffer = storage class 12

Encode every uint32 word as exactly 8 hex characters (little-endian).

Subpass 1: N=1,024 elements
Subpass 2: N=4,096 elements
Subpass 3: N=16,384 elements
Subpass 4: N=65,536 elements

Each uint32 word must be 8 hex digits, little-endian byte order.
The entire binary is one continuous hex string with no spaces or line breaks.

**Task:** Write a compute shader that performs ONE timestep of 3D boid

boundary force when a component exceeds boundSize*0.4 (push toward center

clamp speed to maxSpeed, then update position by vel*dt.

- Guard against gl_GlobalInvocationID.x >= N
- Skip self (i == j) and zero-distance neighbors
- Average the accumulated forces by neighbor count (avoid division by zero)
- Clamp velocity magnitude to maxSpeed

rudder: -1.0 (yaw left) to +1.0 (yaw right)

throttle_2: 0.0 (idle) to 1.0 (full thrust) — right engine

NOTE: If you omit a key, the current value is maintained. Throttle defaults
to the current setting if not specified.

**Critical Design Requirements:**
1. **Sensor fusion**: Cross-check redundant sensors, and cross-check other physical
properties. If GPS altitude is dropping, radar altitude is stable, and barometric
altitude is climbing - two failures have occured, and you have to pick wisely.
2. **Aerodynamic simulation**: The flight model includes a full aerodynamic model, so
brush up on your knowledge of stalls, asymetric thurst, yaw dampening, and trim.

previous values, etc. They persist across calls within a scenario.

Key facts:
- Wheel speed sensors (4): FL, FR, RL, RR in km/h. Any can fail.
- Gyroscopes (3): yaw rate in degrees/second. Any can fail silently.
- Accelerometers (3): longitudinal and lateral in m/s². Any can fail.
- GPS (2): position in meters, speed in km/h. Can lose signal.
- Lidar (12 beams): range in meters at angles from -90° to +90°.
- Vision (3 independent systems): lane line distances, types (solid/dashed),
obstacle detection (bool + distance + relative speed), speed limit signs,
lane offset, road curvature. ANY can fail or flicker!
- `estimated_mu`: estimated tire-road friction (1.0=dry, <0.3=ice).
- `target_speed_kmh`: desired speed. `target_lane`: desired lane (0-2).
- `*_valid` flags exist but may be WRONG on failed sensors.
- Sensors can FLICKER: randomly return invalid data for a few frames.

**Output:** Return a dict:
```
steering: -1.0 (full left) to +1.0 (full right)
0.0 = straight ahead
throttle: 0.0 (no power) to 1.0 (full power)
brake: 0.0 (no brake) to 1.0 (emergency stop)
```
If you omit a key, the current value is maintained.

**Critical Design Requirements:**
1. **Sensor fusion**: Cross-check redundant sensors. Median/voting for disagreements.
2. **Lane keeping**: Stay centered in lane using vision line distances and lidar.
3. **Speed control**: Maintain target speed, respect speed limits.
4. **Obstacle avoidance**: If obstacle detected, brake and/or lane change.
5. **Traction management**: On low-mu surfaces, reduce speed, gentler inputs.
6. **Graceful degradation**: Handle sensor failures, flickering data.
7. **Persistence**: Module-level variables persist across calls for filtering/PID.

**Test Scenarios (25 total):**
0. Normal highway cruise
1. Gentle curve
2. Slow vehicle ahead
3. Emergency stop — stopped vehicle
4. Cut-in from adjacent lane
5. Ice patch — reduced traction
6. Aquaplaning — very low friction
7. Wheel speed sensor failure (FL)
8. Two wheel speed sensors fail
9. Gyro sensor failure
10. GPS signal lost
11. Vision system 1 failure
12. All vision systems flickering
13. Front lidar beams fail
14. Steering angle sensors disagree
15. Total brake failure
16. Throttle stuck at 30%
17. Road debris
18. Dense traffic
19. Crosswind gust
20. Steering partially jammed
21. Ice + stopped vehicle
22. Flickering sensors in curve
23. Reduced visibility
24. Multi-failure + obstacle

Test 53: Spacecraft Orbital Docking Autopilot (Python) Score: 0.00 / 25
Typical Prompt:
Write a Python autopilot to dock a spacecraft with a space station in orbit.

**CRITICAL ORBITAL MECHANICS INSIGHT:**
In orbit, relative motion is COUNTER-INTUITIVE:
- Thrusting TOWARD the target (prograde if behind) raises your orbit → you SLOW DOWN relative to target
- To catch up: thrust RETROGRADE (backward!) to lower orbit → you go FASTER
- Radial thrusts cause oscillation, not direct movement
- Cross-track corrections require thrusts at specific orbital positions
- Near the target (<50m), approximate as linear (CW equations work)
- Far away (>200m), full orbital mechanics dominate

**Function Signature:**
```python
def autopilot_step(state: dict, dt: float) -> dict:
```

Key sensor notes:
- Relative position/velocity in LVLH frame: x=radial (up), y=along-track (velocity dir), z=cross-track
- NEGATIVE y = behind station (most common start). Must CLOSE the y gap.
- Range finders give scalar distance. Radar/lidar give 3D relative pos/vel.
- All sensors can fail silently! Cross-check redundant sensors.
- Docking camera only active within 500m. Gives bearing to docking port.
- Ground station data updates every ~30s (stale but reliable).

```
thrust_x: -1.0 to +1.0 (radial: + = away from Earth)
thrust_y: -1.0 to +1.0 (along-track: + = prograde)
thrust_z: -1.0 to +1.0 (cross-track: + = north)
att_rate_roll: rad/s (max ±0.035)
att_rate_pitch: rad/s (max ±0.035)
att_rate_yaw: rad/s (max ±0.035)
```
Each thrust axis: 220N per thruster, Isp=290s. Fuel is LIMITED (~500 kg).

**Docking Success Criteria:**
- Range < 2m AND relative speed < 0.3 m/s

**Approach Strategy Hints:**
1. Far (>200m): Use Hohmann-like transfer — retrograde to lower orbit if behind
2. Medium (50-200m): Gentle corrections, V-bar approach preferred
3. Close (<50m): Linear regime, direct thrust corrections OK
4. Final (<10m): Very gentle, < 0.1 m/s approach speed

**ILS Approach Key Concepts:**
- `glideslope_N_dots`: deviation from 3° glideslope (+above/-below), 3 receivers
- `localizer_N_dots`: deviation from runway centerline (+right/-left), 3 receivers
- `radio_alt_ft`: height above ground (critical for flare)
- `dme_N_nm`: distance to runway threshold
- `weight_on_wheels`: True when landed
- `target_vref_kt`: reference approach speed (typically 137kt)
- `decision_height_ft`: minimum altitude to continue approach (200ft CAT I)
- Elevator command 0 = trimmed flight. Positive = pitch up.

**Output:** Return a dict with any of:
```
elevator: -1.0 (nose down) to +1.0 (nose up), relative to trim
aileron: -1.0 (roll left) to +1.0 (roll right)
rudder: -1.0 (yaw left) to +1.0 (yaw right)
throttle_1: 0.0 to 1.0 (left engine)
throttle_2: 0.0 to 1.0 (right engine)
elevator_trim: -1.0 to +1.0
flaps: degrees (0-40)
gear: 0.0 (up) or 1.0 (down)
speedbrake: 0.0 (retracted) to 1.0 (full)
spoiler: 0.0 or 1.0 (ground spoilers, deploy after touchdown)
autobrake: 0.0 to 1.0 (braking force after touchdown)
reverse_1: 0.0 to 1.0 (left engine reverse thrust)
reverse_2: 0.0 to 1.0 (right engine reverse thrust)
```

**Approach Phases:**
1. **Intercept** (>1000ft): Track glideslope and localizer, configure for landing
2. **Approach** (1000ft-200ft): Stabilise on glideslope, speed, config
3. **Flare** (<50ft radio alt): Reduce descent rate, idle thrust
4. **Touchdown & Rollout**: Deploy spoilers, reverse thrust, autobrake

**Go-Around:**
If the approach is unstable or unsafe, abort the landing:
- Apply TOGA thrust (throttle 1.0), pitch up, retract speedbrake
- Climb to 1500ft AGL — this completes the go-around
- The sim will then **restart** from a stable approach position with the
**same failures and weather**. Your autopilot must land on the retry.
- Each go-around costs a **0.1 point penalty** on a perfect landing.
- After **10 go-arounds** the scenario fails (score 0.0).

**Scoring:**
- **1.0** — Normal landing: stopped on the runway, or slowed below 50kt
with >30% runway remaining (pilot takes over to taxi).
Minus 0.1 per go-around.
- **0.5** — Hard landing: touchdown vertical speed 360–600 fpm.
Aircraft needs inspection but is reusable, everyone walks away.
- **0.1** — Minor overrun: aircraft rolls off the end but is caught by the
EMAS arrestor bed (within 150m past runway end). Everyone safe,
aircraft damaged.
- **0.0** — Catastrophic: touchdown >600 fpm, major overrun
beyond EMAS, runway excursion, CFIT, or failure to land. Write-off or
loss of life.

**Test Scenarios (25 total):**

1. Short final — 3nm
2. High on glideslope
3. Low on glideslope
4. Offset from centerline
5. Single engine failure on final [Kegworth (1989) / BA 38 (2008)]
6. Windshear on short final [Delta 191 (1985)]

8. Gusty crosswind — 15kt gusting 30
9. CAT III low visibility
10. Slippery wet runway [Overruns at LGA, MDW]
11. Icy runway
12. Glideslope receiver 1+2 failed

15. Elevator partially jammed

18. Heavy weight landing

21. Missed approach required
22. Severe turbulence on final
23. ILS signal flickering
24. Engine failure + crosswind + wet runway [Multiple incidents]

Typical Prompt:
Write a C++ chess bot that for any given chess position, returns the best move to make (or the best
move you can find before the timeout).

You receive the chess position as a string in FEN notation, and you must return the move in
disambiguated algebraic notation (including the starting square, piece type, and destination square).

See:
- https://www.chess.com/terms/fen-chess

Here is an example FEN representing the starting position with white to move:
```
rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1
```

Here is an example disambiguated algebraic move:
```
pe2e4
```
This represents the king's pawn opening - moving the pawn from e2 to e4.

**Move notation rules:**
- Piece letter (lowercase p for pawn, uppercase N/B/R/Q/K for others) + source square + destination square.
- Use "x" between source and destination for captures: `pe4xd5`
- Promotion: append `/` and the piece letter, e.g. `pe7e8/Q`
- Castling: `O-O` (kingside) or `O-O-O` (queenside).
- En passant: append `ep`, e.g. `pe5xd6ep`
- Check: append `+`, e.g. `Bb4c5+`
- Checkmate: append `#`, e.g. `Qd1h5#`

**Input format (stdin, two lines):**
```
timeout_in_seconds
fen_string
```

**Output format (stdout, one line):**
```
move_in_disambiguated_algebraic
```

timeout_in_seconds will be at least 5. Your code will be compiled with full optimisations and
run on a machine with multiple cores, so threading is encouraged.

// Import required modules
const fs = require('fs');

// Function to calculate the Euclidean distance between two points
function distance(x1, y1, x2, y2) {
    return Math.sqrt((x2 - x1) ** 2 + (y2 - y1) ** 2);
}

// Function to solve the vehicle routing problem
function solve(data) {
    const { depot, truckCount, packages } = data;
    const depotX = depot[0];
    const depotY = depot[1];

    // Sort packages by distance from the depot
    packages.sort((a, b) => {
        const distA = distance(depotX, depotY, a.x, a.y);
        const distB = distance(depotX, depotY, b.x, b.y);
        return distA - distB;
    });

    // Assign packages to routes
    const routes = Array(truckCount).fill().map(() => []);
    for (let i = 0; i < packages.length; i++) {
        const packageId = packages[i].id;
        const routeIndex = i % truckCount;
        routes[routeIndex].push(packageId);
    }

    // Filter out empty routes
    const nonEmptyRoutes = routes.filter(route => route.length > 0);

    return { routes: nonEmptyRoutes };
}

// Read input from stdin
const input = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(input);

// Solve the problem and print the result to stdout
const result = solve(data);
console.log(JSON.stringify(result));

const fs = require('fs');

// Read input from stdin
const input = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(input);

// Function to simulate fire spread and calculate the value of towns that would be burned
function simulateFire(grid, width, height, ignitions, towns, firebreaks) {
    // Create a grid to track visited cells
    const visited = Array.from({ length: height }, () => Array(width).fill(false));
    
    // Mark firebreaks and ignitions as visited
    for (const [x, y] of firebreaks) {
        visited[y][x] = true;
    }
    for (const [x, y] of ignitions) {
        visited[y][x] = true;
    }

    // Perform BFS to simulate fire spread
    const queue = [...ignitions];
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const [x, y] = queue.shift();
        for (const [dx, dy] of [[-1, 0], [1, 0], [0, -1], [0, 1]]) {
            const nx = x + dx;
            const ny = y + dy;
            if (nx >= 0 && nx < width && ny >= 0 && ny < height && !visited[ny][nx] && grid[ny][nx] === '.') {
                visited[ny][nx] = true;
                queue.push([nx, ny]);
            }
        }
    }

    // Calculate the value of towns that would be burned
    let burnedValue = 0;
    for (const town of towns) {
        if (visited[town.y][town.x]) {
            burnedValue += town.value;
        }
    }
    return burnedValue;
}

// Main function to determine the optimal firebreaks
function determineFirebreaks(data) {
    const { width, height, grid, ignitions, towns, cutBudget } = data;
    const firebreaks = [];

    // Simulate initial fire spread to identify cells that are reachable by fire
    const initialBurnedValue = simulateFire(grid, width, height, ignitions, towns, []);

    // If no towns are burned, return empty firebreaks
    if (initialBurnedValue === 0) {
        return { firebreaks };
    }

    // Create a priority queue to store cells to be considered for firebreaks
    const queue = [];
    for (const [x, y] of ignitions) {
        for (const [dx, dy] of [[-1, 0], [1, 0], [0, -1], [0, 1]]) {
            const nx = x + dx;
            const ny = y + dy;
            if (nx >= 0 && nx < width && ny >= 0 && ny < height && grid[ny][nx] === '.') {
                queue.push([nx, ny, 0]); // [x, y, distance]
            }
        }
    }

    // Perform a greedy search to find the optimal firebreaks
    while (queue.length > 0 && cutBudget > 0) {
        queue.sort((a, b) => {
            // Prioritize cells that are closer to ignitions and have higher town value saved
            const valueSavedA = simulateFire(grid, width, height, ignitions, towns, [...firebreaks, [a[0], a[1]]]) - initialBurnedValue;
            const valueSavedB = simulateFire(grid, width, height, ignitions, towns, [...firebreaks, [b[0], b[1]]]) - initialBurnedValue;
            return valueSavedB - valueSavedA || a[2] - b[2];
        });
        const [x, y, distance] = queue.shift();
        if (grid[y][x] === '.' && !firebreaks.some(([fx, fy]) => fx === x && fy === y)) {
            firebreaks.push([x, y]);
            cutBudget--;
            // Update the queue with new neighbors
            for (const [dx, dy] of [[-1, 0], [1, 0], [0, -1], [0, 1]]) {
                const nx = x + dx;
                const ny = y + dy;
                if (nx >= 0 && nx < width && ny >= 0 && ny < height && grid[ny][nx] === '.') {
                    queue.push([nx, ny, distance + 1]);
                }
            }
        }
    }

    return { firebreaks };
}

// Determine and output the optimal firebreaks
const result = determineFirebreaks(data);
console.log(JSON.stringify(result));

const fs = require('fs');

// Read input from stdin
const input = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(input);

// Define a function to calculate Manhattan distance between two points
function manhattanDistance(x1, y1, x2, y2) {
    return Math.abs(x1 - x2) + Math.abs(y1 - y2);
}

// Assign jobs to robots based on the nearest robot
function assignJobs(robots, jobs) {
    // Create a copy of the jobs array to avoid modifying the original array
    const remainingJobs = [...jobs];

    // Sort the jobs by priority in descending order
    remainingJobs.sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority);

    // Initialize an array to store the assigned jobs for each robot
    const assignments = Array(robots.length).fill().map(() => []);

    // Assign jobs to the nearest robot
    while (remainingJobs.length > 0) {
        const job = remainingJobs.shift();
        let nearestRobotIndex = -1;
        let minDistance = Infinity;

        // Find the nearest robot to the current job
        for (let i = 0; i < robots.length; i++) {
            const distance = manhattanDistance(robots[i].x, robots[i].y, job.x, job.y);
            if (distance < minDistance) {
                minDistance = distance;
                nearestRobotIndex = i;
            }
        }

        // Assign the job to the nearest robot
        assignments[nearestRobotIndex].push(job.id);
    }

    return assignments;
}

// Process the input data
function processInput(data) {
    const robots = data.robots;
    const jobs = data.jobs;

    // Assign jobs to robots
    const assignments = assignJobs(robots, jobs);

    // Return the assignments in the required format
    return { assignments };
}

// Output the result to stdout
const output = processInput(data);
console.log(JSON.stringify(output));

const fs = require('fs');

// Read input from stdin
const input = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(input);

// Extract input data
const probability = data.probability;
const drones = data.drones;
const maxStepsPerDrone = data.maxStepsPerDrone;

// Define grid dimensions
const gridHeight = probability.length;
const gridWidth = probability[0].length;

// Define possible movements (up, down, left, right, stay)
const movements = [[-1, 0], [1, 0], [0, -1], [0, 1], [0, 0]];

// Function to check if a cell is valid (inside grid and not an obstacle)
function isValidCell(x, y) {
    return x >= 0 && x < gridHeight && y >= 0 && y < gridWidth && probability[x][y] !== -1;
}

// Function to plan a path for a drone using a greedy approach
function planPath(drone) {
    const path = [[drone.x, drone.y]];
    let currentX = drone.x;
    let currentY = drone.y;

    for (let step = 0; step < maxStepsPerDrone; step++) {
        let bestMovement = null;
        let bestValue = -Infinity;

        for (const movement of movements) {
            const newX = currentX + movement[0];
            const newY = currentY + movement[1];

            if (isValidCell(newX, newY)) {
                const newValue = probability[newX][newY];
                if (newValue > bestValue) {
                    bestValue = newValue;
                    bestMovement = movement;
                }
            }
        }

        if (bestMovement !== null) {
            currentX += bestMovement[0];
            currentY += bestMovement[1];
            path.push([currentX, currentY]);
        } else {
            // If no valid movement is found, stay in place
            path.push([currentX, currentY]);
        }
    }

    return path;
}

// Plan paths for all drones
const paths = drones.map(planPath);

// Output the result as JSON
console.log(JSON.stringify({ paths }));

Approach: **Mission Control Work Scheduler** ===================================== This Node.js program schedules mission-control work across parallel workstations based on the given input JSON. **Code** --------

View JavaScript code (2273 chars)
const fs = require('fs');

// Read input from stdin
const input = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(input);

// Extract machine count and tasks
const { machineCount, tasks } = data;

// Create a map to store tasks by their IDs
const taskMap = new Map();
tasks.forEach((task) => taskMap.set(task.id, task));

// Perform topological sorting
const visited = new Set();
const order = [];
const visiting = new Set();

function topologicalSort(taskId) {
    if (visiting.has(taskId)) {
        throw new Error("Cycle detected in task dependencies");
    }
    if (visited.has(taskId)) {
        return;
    }
    visiting.add(taskId);
    const task = taskMap.get(taskId);
    task.deps.forEach((dep) => topologicalSort(dep));
    visiting.delete(taskId);
    visited.add(taskId);
    order.push(taskId);
}

tasks.forEach((task) => {
    if (!visited.has(task.id)) {
        topologicalSort(task.id);
    }
});

// Sort tasks based on their deadlines and weights
order.sort((a, b) => {
    const taskA = taskMap.get(a);
    const taskB = taskMap.get(b);
    // Prioritize tasks with earlier deadlines and higher weights
    if (taskA.deadline !== taskB.deadline) {
        return taskA.deadline - taskB.deadline;
    } else {
        return taskB.weight - taskA.weight;
    }
});

// Assign tasks to machines greedily
const machineTasks = Array(machineCount).fill(0).map(() => []);
order.forEach((taskId) => {
    const task = taskMap.get(taskId);
    // Find the machine that is available the earliest
    let minMachine = 0;
    let minTime = machineTasks[0].reduce((sum, t) => sum + taskMap.get(t).duration, 0);
    for (let i = 1; i < machineCount; i++) {
        const time = machineTasks[i].reduce((sum, t) => sum + taskMap.get(t).duration, 0);
        if (time < minTime) {
            minMachine = i;
            minTime = time;
        }
    }
    machineTasks[minMachine].push(taskId);
});

// Create the schedule
const schedule = [];
machineTasks.forEach((taskIds, machineIndex) => {
    let time = 0;
    taskIds.forEach((taskId) => {
        schedule.push({ id: taskId, start: time, machine: machineIndex });
        time += taskMap.get(taskId).duration;
    });
});

// Output the schedule in JSON format
console.log(JSON.stringify({ schedule }));

Approach: # Delivery Route Planner ## Overview This TypeScript program plans delivery routes for a fleet of vans. It takes a JSON input containing the depot location, the maximum number of vans, and a list of packages with their locations. The program outputs a JSON document describing the planned routes. ## Code

View TypeScript code (1462 chars)
// Import required modules
declare const require: any;
const fs = require('fs');

// Read input from stdin
const input: string = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(input);

// Define types
interface Package {
  id: string;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

interface InputData {
  depot: [number, number];
  truckCount: number;
  packages: Package[];
}

interface Route {
  route: string[];
}

// Function to calculate the distance between two points
function distance(x1: number, y1: number, x2: number, y2: number): number {
  return Math.sqrt((x2 - x1) ** 2 + (y2 - y1) ** 2);
}

// Function to solve the delivery route planning problem
function planDeliveryRoutes(data: InputData): { routes: string[][] } {
  const { depot, truckCount, packages } = data;
  const depotX = depot[0];
  const depotY = depot[1];

  // Sort packages by distance from the depot
  packages.sort((a, b) => {
    const distA = distance(depotX, depotY, a.x, a.y);
    const distB = distance(depotX, depotY, b.x, b.y);
    return distA - distB;
  });

  // Assign packages to routes
  const routes: string[][] = Array.from({ length: truckCount }, () => []);
  for (let i = 0; i < packages.length; i++) {
    const packageId = packages[i].id;
    const routeIndex = i % truckCount;
    routes[routeIndex].push(packageId);
  }

  return { routes };
}

// Plan delivery routes and output the result
const result = planDeliveryRoutes(data);
console.log(JSON.stringify(result));

import * as fs from 'fs';

// Function to read input from stdin
function readInput(): string {
    return fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
}

// Function to simulate fire spread and calculate the score
function simulateFireSpread(grid: string[][], width: number, height: number, ignitions: number[][], towns: { id: any; x: number; y: number; value: number }[], firebreaks: number[][]): number {
    // Create a copy of the grid to simulate fire spread
    const fireGrid: boolean[][] = Array.from({ length: height }, () => new Array(width).fill(false));

    // Mark ignition points as burned
    for (const [x, y] of ignitions) {
        fireGrid[y][x] = true;
    }

    // Simulate fire spread
    const directions: number[][] = [[0, 1], [0, -1], [1, 0], [-1, 0]];
    let queue: number[][] = [...ignitions];
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const newQueue: number[][] = [];
        for (const [x, y] of queue) {
            for (const [dx, dy] of directions) {
                const nx: number = x + dx;
                const ny: number = y + dy;
                if (nx >= 0 && nx < width && ny >= 0 && ny < height && grid[ny][nx] === '.' && !fireGrid[ny][nx]) {
                    let isFirebreak: boolean = false;
                    for (const [fx, fy] of firebreaks) {
                        if (fx === nx && fy === ny) {
                            isFirebreak = true;
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                    if (!isFirebreak) {
                        fireGrid[ny][nx] = true;
                        newQueue.push([nx, ny]);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        queue = newQueue;
    }

    // Calculate the score
    let savedValue: number = 0;
    let totalBurnedValue: number = 0;
    for (const town of towns) {
        if (fireGrid[town.y][town.x]) {
            totalBurnedValue += town.value;
        } else {
            savedValue += town.value;
        }
    }

    return totalBurnedValue > 0 ? savedValue / (savedValue + totalBurnedValue) : 1;
}

// Function to choose firebreaks
function chooseFirebreaks(data: any): number[][] {
    const width: number = data.width;
    const height: number = data.height;
    const grid: string[] = data.grid;
    const ignitions: number[][] = data.ignitions;
    const towns: { id: any; x: number; y: number; value: number }[] = data.towns;
    const cutBudget: number = data.cutBudget;

    // Convert grid to 2D array
    const grid2D: string[][] = Array.from({ length: height }, (_, y) => grid.slice(y * width, (y + 1) * width));

    // Simulate fire spread without firebreaks to identify cells that will be burned
    const fireGrid: boolean[][] = Array.from({ length: height }, () => new Array(width).fill(false));
    for (const [x, y] of ignitions) {
        fireGrid[y][x] = true;
    }
    const directions: number[][] = [[0, 1], [0, -1], [1, 0], [-1, 0]];
    let queue: number[][] = [...ignitions];
    while (queue.length > 0) {
        const newQueue: number[][] = [];
        for (const [x, y] of queue) {
            for (const [dx, dy] of directions) {
                const nx: number = x + dx;
                const ny: number = y + dy;
                if (nx >= 0 && nx < width && ny >= 0 && ny < height && grid2D[ny][nx] === '.' && !fireGrid[ny][nx]) {
                    fireGrid[ny][nx] = true;
                    newQueue.push([nx, ny]);
                }
            }
        }
        queue = newQueue;
    }

    // Identify cells that are adjacent to burned cells and are burnable
    const candidates: number[][] = [];
    for (let y = 0; y < height; y++) {
        for (let x = 0; x < width; x++) {
            if (grid2D[y][x] === '.') {
                for (const [dx, dy] of directions) {
                    const nx: number = x + dx;
                    const ny: number = y + dy;
                    if (nx >= 0 && nx < width && ny >= 0 && ny < height && fireGrid[ny][nx]) {
                        candidates.push([x, y]);
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // Choose firebreaks
    const firebreaks: number[][] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < cutBudget && i < candidates.length; i++) {
        firebreaks.push(candidates[i]);
    }

    return firebreaks;
}

// Main function
function main(): void {
    const input: string = readInput();
    const data = JSON.parse(input);
    const firebreaks: number[][] = chooseFirebreaks(data);
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ firebreaks }));
}

main();

Approach: # Robot Job Assignment ## Problem Statement Assign warehouse pick jobs to robots based on the shortest grid walking distance. ## Solution The following TypeScript program reads the input JSON from stdin, processes it, and outputs the assignments to stdout.

View TypeScript code (2730 chars)
import * as fs from 'fs';

// Define the input data structure
interface Robot {
  id: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

interface Job {
  id: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
  priority: number;
}

interface InputData {
  grid: string[];
  robots: Robot[];
  jobs: Job[];
}

// Define the output data structure
interface OutputData {
  assignments: number[][];
}

// Function to calculate Manhattan distance between two points
function manhattanDistance(x1: number, y1: number, x2: number, y2: number): number {
  return Math.abs(x1 - x2) + Math.abs(y1 - y2);
}

// Function to check if a cell is valid (not blocked and within grid bounds)
function isValidCell(grid: string[], x: number, y: number): boolean {
  return x >= 0 && x < grid.length && y >= 0 && y < grid[0].length && grid[x][y] !== '#';
}

// Function to calculate the shortest distance between a robot and a job using BFS
function calculateDistance(grid: string[], robotX: number, robotY: number, jobX: number, jobY: number): number {
  const queue: [number, number, number][] = [[robotX, robotY, 0]];
  const visited: boolean[][] = Array(grid.length).fill(false).map(() => Array(grid[0].length).fill(false));
  visited[robotX][robotY] = true;

  while (queue.length > 0) {
    const [x, y, distance] = queue.shift()!;
    if (x === jobX && y === jobY) {
      return distance;
    }

    // Explore neighbors
    for (const [dx, dy] of [[-1, 0], [1, 0], [0, -1], [0, 1]]) {
      const nx = x + dx;
      const ny = y + dy;
      if (isValidCell(grid, nx, ny) && !visited[nx][ny]) {
        queue.push([nx, ny, distance + 1]);
        visited[nx][ny] = true;
      }
    }
  }

  // If there's no path, return infinity
  return Infinity;
}

// Main function to assign jobs to robots
function assignJobs(data: InputData): OutputData {
  const assignments: number[][] = Array(data.robots.length).fill(0).map(() => []);

  // Sort jobs by priority in descending order
  data.jobs.sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority);

  for (const job of data.jobs) {
    let closestRobot: number | null = null;
    let minDistance = Infinity;

    for (const robot of data.robots) {
      const distance = calculateDistance(data.grid, robot.x, robot.y, job.x, job.y);
      if (distance < minDistance) {
        minDistance = distance;
        closestRobot = robot.id;
      }
    }

    if (closestRobot !== null) {
      assignments[closestRobot].push(job.id);
    }
  }

  return { assignments };
}

// Read input from stdin
const input: string = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data: InputData = JSON.parse(input);

// Process the input data and generate output
const output: OutputData = assignJobs(data);

// Write output to stdout
console.log(JSON.stringify(output));

Drone Search Coverage Planner - 2 drones, 55 steps

View TypeScript code (2149 chars)
import * as fs from 'fs';

// Define the input and output interfaces
interface InputData {
  probability: number[][];
  drones: { id: number; x: number; y: number }[];
  maxStepsPerDrone: number;
}

interface OutputData {
  paths: number[][][];
}

// Read input from stdin
const input: string = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data: InputData = JSON.parse(input);

// Define the grid dimensions
const gridHeight = data.probability.length;
const gridWidth = data.probability[0].length;

// Define the possible movements (up, down, left, right, stay)
const movements: [number, number][] = [
  [-1, 0],
  [1, 0],
  [0, -1],
  [0, 1],
  [0, 0],
];

// Function to check if a cell is valid (inside the grid and not an obstacle)
function isValidCell(x: number, y: number): boolean {
  return x >= 0 && x < gridHeight && y >= 0 && y < gridWidth && data.probability[x][y] !== -1;
}

// Function to plan a path for a drone using a greedy approach
function planPath(droneX: number, droneY: number, maxSteps: number): number[][] {
  const path: number[][] = [[droneX, droneY]];
  let currentX = droneX;
  let currentY = droneY;

  for (let step = 0; step < maxSteps; step++) {
    let bestMovement: [number, number] | null = null;
    let bestValue = -Infinity;

    for (const movement of movements) {
      const newX = currentX + movement[0];
      const newY = currentY + movement[1];

      if (isValidCell(newX, newY)) {
        const newValue = data.probability[newX][newY];
        if (newValue > bestValue) {
          bestValue = newValue;
          bestMovement = movement;
        }
      }
    }

    if (bestMovement !== null) {
      currentX += bestMovement[0];
      currentY += bestMovement[1];
      path.push([currentX, currentY]);
    } else {
      // If no valid movement is found, stay in place
      path.push([currentX, currentY]);
    }
  }

  return path;
}

// Plan paths for all drones
const paths: number[][][] = data.drones.map((drone) =>
  planPath(drone.x, drone.y, data.maxStepsPerDrone)
);

// Create the output data
const output: OutputData = { paths };

// Print the output to stdout
console.log(JSON.stringify(output));

Space Mission Work Schedule - 24 tasks, 3 workstations

Approach: # Mission Control Work Scheduler ## Overview This Node.js TypeScript program schedules mission-control work across parallel workstations. It takes a JSON input containing the number of machines and a list of tasks with their dependencies, durations, deadlines, and weights. The program outputs a JSON document representing either a detailed schedule or a topological order of tasks. ## Code

View TypeScript code (1713 chars)
import * as fs from 'fs';

// Define the input and output data structures
interface Task {
  id: string;
  duration: number;
  deps: string[];
  deadline: number;
  weight: number;
}

interface InputData {
  machineCount: number;
  tasks: Task[];
}

interface ScheduleOutput {
  schedule: { id: string; start: number; machine: number }[];
}

interface OrderOutput {
  order: string[];
}

// Read input from stdin
const input: string = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
const data: InputData = JSON.parse(input);

// Process tasks
const taskMap: Map<string, Task> = new Map();
for (const task of data.tasks) {
  taskMap.set(task.id, task);
}

// Build graph and in-degree map
const graph: Map<string, string[]> = new Map();
const inDegree: Map<string, number> = new Map();
for (const task of data.tasks) {
  inDegree.set(task.id, task.deps.length);
  for (const dep of task.deps) {
    if (!graph.has(dep)) {
      graph.set(dep, []);
    }
    graph.get(dep)!.push(task.id);
  }
}

// Topological sorting using Kahn's algorithm
const order: string[] = [];
const queue: string[] = data.tasks.filter((task) => inDegree.get(task.id)! === 0).map((task) => task.id);
while (queue.length > 0) {
  const taskId = queue.shift()!;
  order.push(taskId);
  if (graph.has(taskId)) {
    for (const neighbor of graph.get(taskId)!) {
      const degree = inDegree.get(neighbor)! - 1;
      inDegree.set(neighbor, degree);
      if (degree === 0) {
        queue.push(neighbor);
      }
    }
  }
}

// Check for cycles
if (order.length !== data.tasks.length) {
  throw new Error("Cycle detected in the task dependencies");
}

// Output the topological order
const output: OrderOutput = { order };
console.log(JSON.stringify(output));
